CLASS 24 · AGES 4–5 · 32 SPOTTER-CARD LESSONS

Transportation & Vehicles.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Thirty-two spotter cards, four vehicles each, one spotting habit.

Every card in this class is a spotter sheet: a group heading — Land, Water, Air or Construction Vehicles — over four labeled vehicles, and every tile below opens its own step-by-step lesson teaching all four. The order is deliberate: the rides your child already takes come first (car, bus, train, bicycle), then the helper trucks that keep a town running, the rails and the long giants, the boats, the flyers and eleven sheets of construction giants from road roller to tower crane. Each lesson ends with one spotting idea — a hunt, a count, a sort — that carries the words out to real traffic.

Class 24 has been reserved since the school opened; the owner assigned it to Transportation & Vehicles, so the learning path now runs from Class 1 to Class 37 with no gap. One card a sitting is plenty — the whole class is a term of five-minute spotting visits, and the words go with the art: every vehicle named in a lesson is printed on its card.

WHY VEHICLES MATTER

Things that go, thinking that grows.

Vehicles are the friendliest gateway to reasoning a preschooler meets: every body is the answer to a job. Why is the race car pointy? Speed. Why is the armored vehicle slow? Protection. Why does the bus bend in the middle? Corners. The class teaches the questions, and the questions travel — to spoons, chairs, raincoats and every shaped thing the world hands over next.

And the spotting habit is the quiet engine: a child who hunts buses, tractors and tower cranes from the window is doing observation, classification and counting in one game. By the end, your child has thirty-two spotter cards, one hundred and twenty-eight named vehicles and a street that has become a field trip.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Car, Bus, Train & Bicycle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens Class 24 with the four rides almost every family meets in one week — and turns them into a spotting habit that runs all term.

What is this?

Car, bus, train and bicycle are the anchor vehicles of the transport theme: one private, one public, one on rails, one on legs. Every other card in this class is a cousin of one of these four.

What does it mean?

Children learn categories by anchoring: the car anchors "roads," the train anchors "rails," the bus anchors "shared rides," the bicycle anchors "people power." Every new vehicle lands on a familiar hook.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a window with a view or a walk planned, and the four names said slowly. The hunt — spot one of each — can take a week. That is the point.

Why this matters

These four are personal: the family car, the school bus, the bike in the yard. Vocabulary anchored in a child’s own life sticks — which is why this card opens the class.

What it teaches

Category anchoring (road/rail/people-power), counting wheels, first-person narrative ("WE ride the bus"), and the observation habit that spotting builds.

Words to learn

carbustrainbicycleridewheelstracks

Say this to your child

“"Car! Bus! Train! Bicycle! The car is ours, the bus carries everyone, the train runs on its tracks, and the bicycle goes on YOUR power. This week we hunt all four — who spots the train first?"”

Step by step

  1. Name the four, one by one: "car — WE ride in a car. Bus — it carries lots of people. Train — it runs on tracks. Bicycle — YOUR legs make it go."
  2. The wheel count: car four, bus six, train MANY, bicycle two. Count them on the card.
  3. The ride report: "how did YOU get here today? Who came by bus?" Every answer is a word landing.
  4. Set the hunt: "this week, spot all four! A car… a bus… a train… a bicycle. Tell me each time!"
  5. Debrief at the end of the week: which was hardest to find? (Usually the train — a good reason to visit the station.)

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over four labeled pictures: a blue car, a city bus, a fast train and a bicycle — the everyday fleet, drawn bright.

Ask your child

"Which one have YOU ridden?" "How many wheels on each?" "What makes a train different?" (the tracks!) "Which will we spot first?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might report every family ride, count wheels on sighted cars, or demand the station visit — the anchor words, working.

Out in the real world

All four live on your street: cars everywhere, a bus stop, a bike rack, tracks across town. The card turns errands into field work.

Try it together

Ride Bingo: a hand-drawn card with four squares — car, bus, train, bicycle. Fill the card by the weekend. Winner picks the next walk’s route.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the four rides." "Which runs on tracks?" "Which one needs YOUR legs?" — four names, one rails answer, one legs answer: anchored.

This lesson pairs with the Car, Bus, Train & Bicycle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Truck, Motorcycle, Tractor & Ambulance — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the big idea that vehicles are tools: the truck hauls, the motorcycle zips, the tractor pulls, the ambulance rushes — each body shaped by its work.

What is this?

Four working vehicles: a cargo truck, a motorcycle, a farm tractor and an ambulance — each designed for exactly one kind of job.

What does it mean?

"Vehicles are tools" is the deepest idea in the transport theme: it turns naming into reasoning. Why does the tractor have huge wheels? Ask its job. Why is the ambulance white with a siren? Ask its job.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the job list: haul, zip, pull, help. Match each vehicle to its verb, then hunt for real examples doing real jobs.

Why this matters

Job-matching is the first step from naming to explaining — the thinking skill that makes the whole rest of the class make sense.

What it teaches

Function reasoning (shape follows job), verb vocabulary (haul, pull, rush), community-helpers seeding (the ambulance’s crew), and sorting.

Words to learn

truckmotorcycletractorambulancehaulpullrush

Say this to your child

“"Truck! Motorcycle! Tractor! Ambulance! The truck hauls, the motorcycle zips, the tractor pulls, the ambulance rushes to help. Every vehicle has a JOB — and its body is the answer. What job do you see?"”

Step by step

  1. Four names first: "truck… motorcycle… tractor… ambulance."
  2. The verb match: "who HAULS furniture? (truck) Who ZIPS through traffic? (motorcycle) Who PULLS the plow? (tractor) who RUSHES to help? (ambulance)"
  3. The why-shape question: "why does the tractor have such BIG wheels?" — muddy fields! The job wrote the body.
  4. The helper hand-off: "the ambulance is a first-aid kit with wheels — who rides inside?" (paramedics — see Class 33!)
  5. The road hunt: spot a truck hauling, a tractor (or a mower!), an ambulance’s lights. Jobs, everywhere.

Look closer at the picture

On this card four labeled pictures sit under the heading "Land": a blue truck, a motorcycle, an orange tractor and a white-and-blue ambulance.

Ask your child

"Who hauls? Who pulls?" "Why big wheels on the tractor?" "What does the ambulance do — and who drives it?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might assign jobs to every vehicle in sight, explain the tractor’s wheels to grandma, or siren-imitate the ambulance — tool thinking, running.

Out in the real world

Working vehicles are everywhere: delivery vans on the street, tractors past the town edge, ambulances on call. Jobs fill the road.

Try it together

Job Sort: toy vehicles vs picture cards — match each to a job card (haul/zip/pull/help). Wrong matches are funnier and more instructive than right ones.

Understanding check

Ask: "Match the four to their jobs." "Why is the ambulance fast?" "What pulls the plow?" — verbs landing on the right wheels: tool thinking, installed.

This lesson pairs with the Truck, Motorcycle, Tractor & Ambulance flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Tram, Trolleybus, Rickshaw & Cable Car — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the city movers that cannot steer: the tram rides rails in the road, the trolleybus holds a stick to the wire, the rickshaw weaves, the cable car climbs on a rope.

What is this?

Four guided vehicles: tram (rails), trolleybus (overhead wire), rickshaw (three wheels, a roof, a horn) and cable car (hanging from a moving rope).

What does it mean?

"Guided vehicles" is a category children can SEE: rails you can touch, wires you can trace, ropes you can follow up a mountain. The city’s tracks hide in plain sight.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the follow-the-line question for each: what does the tram follow? (rails) The trolleybus? (the wire) The cable car? (the rope) The rickshaw? (only its driver!)

Why this matters

Spotting the hidden lines — rails in the tarmac, wires over the street — turns every city walk into an engineering tour. And the rickshaw belongs to millions of families who ride one daily.

What it teaches

Observation of infrastructure, category building (guided vs free), local-transport pride (the rickshaw!), and the guided/free distinction.

Words to learn

tramtrolleybusrickshawcable carrailswirerope

Say this to your child

“"Tram! Trolleybus! Rickshaw! Cable car! The tram rides its rails, the trolleybus holds the wire’s stick, the cable car climbs on a rope — and the rickshaw goes ANYWHERE its driver wants. Which city mover would you ride?"”

Step by step

  1. Four names: "tram… trolleybus… rickshaw… cable car."
  2. The follow question, one by one: "what does the tram follow? RAILS in the road! The trolleybus? A wire — see the stick on its roof! The cable car? A ROPE up the mountain."
  3. The odd one out: "the rickshaw follows NOTHING — its driver steers anywhere! Why is it on this card?" (Discuss — it is the free spirit.)
  4. The walk challenge: find a tram rail, a trolleybus wire, or a cable car this week.
  5. The ride poll: which one would you ride first — and why?

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a blue tram, a trolleybus with its roof pole, a three-wheeled rickshaw and a cable car on its line — city transport, four ways.

Ask your child

"What does each one follow?" "Which one steers freely?" (the rickshaw!) "Which would you ride up a mountain?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might trace tram rails on a walk, spot the trolleybus sticks overhead, or narrate a rickshaw ride from memory — the lines, found.

Out in the real world

Cities worldwide run all four: trams in Melbourne, trolleybuses in Sofia, rickshaws in Lahore and Dhaka, cable cars in the Alps and Rio. A postcard tour is one conversation long.

Try it together

Guided Line Hunt: on your next walk, count the guided lines you can find — rails, wires, painted lanes. Record the finds with a tally; the city is more built than anyone noticed.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the tram follow?" (rails) "What holds the trolleybus to its wire?" (the stick) "Who steers the rickshaw?" (its driver!)

This lesson pairs with the Tram, Trolleybus, Rickshaw & Cable Car flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fire Engine, Police Car, Tow Truck & Garbage Truck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the helper fleet: the trucks children love loudest, each doing a job that keeps a town safe, moving and clean.

What is this?

Four community vehicles: fire engine (fires and rescues), police car (safety), tow truck (broken cars) and garbage truck (the weekly crunch).

What does it mean?

Helper vehicles are the bridge between this class and the community-helpers class: truck + job + the person who drives it. They are also the easiest kindness lesson with wheels on.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the four jobs: fight fire, keep safe, rescue cars, take trash. The siren question — "why do they make noise?" — is the depth: to tell everyone to make way for help.

Why this matters

Children admire these trucks; admiration is a doorway. Walking through it lands the biggest idea in the theme: vehicles exist to help people.

What it teaches

Community-job vocabulary, siren meaning (make way!), sequencing the garbage truck’s weekly visit, and the helper identity that Class 33 grows.

Words to learn

fire enginepolice cartow truckgarbage truckhelpsirenrescue

Say this to your child

“"Fire engine! Police car! Tow truck! Garbage truck! The helpers of our town — fighting fires, keeping us safe, rescuing cars, taking the trash. And the siren says: make way — help is coming! Who are the helpers in YOUR street?"”

Step by step

  1. Four names and four jobs: "fire engine — fights fires. Police car — keeps us safe. Tow truck — rescues broken cars. Garbage truck — takes the trash away. CRUNCH."
  2. The siren question: "why the loud noise? So everyone hears: HELP IS COMING — make way!"
  3. The weekly rhythm: "which helper visits OUR street? When? Let’s watch for it!"
  4. The gratitude beat: "who drives them? Firefighters, police officers, the tow driver, the bin crew — helpers with trucks."
  5. The spotting week: every helper truck seen gets its name called out. The loudest game in the class.

Look closer at the picture

On this card four labeled trucks sit under the heading "Land": a red fire engine, a police car, a tow truck and a green garbage truck — the town’s fleet.

Ask your child

"Match each truck to its job." "Why do helpers have sirens?" "Which helper visits your street — and when?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might narrate the garbage truck’s whole visit, siren through the house for stuffed animals, or thank a real firefighter — helpers, honoured.

Out in the real world

Helper trucks run on a schedule you can watch: bin day, the fire station open day, the tow truck at the corner. Real helpers beat any worksheet.

Try it together

Helper Rescue: teddy stuck on the "roof" (sofa back) — the toy fire engine and its crew respond. Sirens optional; the ladder (your arm) essential. Rotate the emergencies; rotate the heroes.

Understanding check

Ask: "Match the four trucks to their jobs." "What does the siren mean?" (make way — help coming) "Who drives them?" (helpers!)

This lesson pairs with the Fire Engine, Police Car, Tow Truck & Garbage Truck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Scooter, Skateboard, Roller Skates & Unicycle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the powered-by-you family: no engine, no fuel, just the rider — and a wheel count that runs from eight all the way down to one.

What is this?

Four rider-powered rides: kick scooter (two wheels), skateboard (four), roller skates (eight) and unicycle (one glorious wheel).

What does it mean?

No-engine transport is the bridge to the sports class: these four ARE balance and push skills. The wheel countdown — two, four, eight… ONE — is the maths hook.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, the wheel count and one leg: the unicycle’s secret is single-leg balance, which every child can practise on the floor with shoes on.

Why this matters

The unicycle’s "one" is the punchline children retell for weeks — and the balance practice behind it is genuinely useful for every ride to come.

What it teaches

Counting down (8-4-2-1), single-leg balance, push-glide rhythm, and the engine-vs-legs category split.

Words to learn

scooterskateboardroller skatesunicyclebalanceglide

Say this to your child

“"Scooter — two wheels! Skateboard — four! Roller skates — eight! Unicycle… ONE. No engine — just YOU: kick, push, clip-clop, balance. Show me your one-wheel balance — wobbling is practicing! And helmets on, always."”

Step by step

  1. Names and wheel counts: "scooter — two. Skateboard — four. Roller skates — EIGHT. Unicycle… ONE!"
  2. The countdown game: hold up fingers — the child names the ride with that many wheels. One finger = chaos and delight.
  3. The balance lab: stand on one leg like a unicycle rider — five seconds each side, arms out, wobbles welcome.
  4. The push demo: how does a scooter go? A KICK. How does a skateboard go? A PUSH. All four run on the rider.
  5. The safety line: "every one of these wears a helmet — even the unicycle. Especially the unicycle."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a kick scooter, a skateboard, a pair of roller skates and a unicycle — the you-powered family, wheel counts shown.

Ask your child

"Order them by wheels — most to least." "What powers all four?" (the rider!) "Show me unicycle balance!"

What your child can say or do

Your child might count wheels on every scooter at the park, balance on one leg through the hallway, or request the unicycle "for my birthday" — you-power, internalized.

Out in the real world

The park is the exhibit: scooters, boards and skates in action. Watch one minute and count the pushes — the engine is always a leg.

Try it together

Wheel-Count Relay: cards face down, flip, shout the wheel count, do that many hops. Eight hops for roller skates — the workout is built in.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many wheels on each?" "What powers them?" (the rider!) "Show me the one-wheel balance!" — counts, power, balance: the family is learned.

This lesson pairs with the Scooter, Skateboard, Roller Skates & Unicycle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Van, Minibus, Limousine & Convertible — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the car family: one basic car, four different bodies — boxy for cargo, long for stars, roofless for sunshine — and the design question behind every shape.

What is this?

Four cars: delivery van (box for cargo), minibus (seats for a team), limousine (stretched long) and convertible (roof down).

What does it mean?

Same basic machine, four answers to four jobs — this is design thinking in vehicle form. The limousine’s length and the convertible’s missing roof both have REASONS.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the question that unlocks it: "what is it carrying?" Boxes, people, stars, sunshine — the answer explains every body.

Why this matters

Children who ask "why is it shaped that way?" start reasoning about design everywhere — spoons, chairs, raincoats. The car family is the friendliest first example.

What it teaches

Design reasoning (shape follows purpose), carry-sorting (cargo vs people), length comparison, and the spotting vocabulary of real traffic.

Words to learn

vanminibuslimousineconvertiblecargostretchedroof

Say this to your child

“"Van! Minibus! Limousine! Convertible! Same car — four bodies: boxes, teams, stars and sunshine. WHY is the limousine long? Its job says so! Design your own — what does YOUR car carry?"”

Step by step

  1. Four bodies: "van — a box on wheels for PACKAGES. Minibus — seats for a whole TEAM. Limousine — a car stretched LOOOONG. Convertible — the roof comes OFF!"
  2. The carry question: "what is each one carrying?" Sort aloud: boxes, team, stars, sunshine.
  3. The why: "WHY is the limousine long? For stretching out! WHY no roof? For sunshine! Every shape has a reason."
  4. The street test: next drive, spot all four. Vans are easy; the limousine is the jackpot.
  5. The design challenge: "design YOUR car — what does it carry? Draw it!" (The canvas on this lesson is exactly for this.)

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a blue van, a minibus, a long white limousine and a convertible with its top down — one idea, four bodies.

Ask your child

"What does each car carry?" "Why is one stretched?" "Why has one no roof?" "What would YOUR car carry?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might classify every parked car, sketch a limousine six pages long, or explain convertibles to a sibling — design eyes, open.

Out in the real world

The school run is a museum: vans delivering, minibuses shuttling, the occasional convertible with its roof arguing with the weather. All four in one week.

Try it together

Car Factory: one toy car chassis, four "bodies" built from boxes — swap the body, change the job. The factory ships all four by lunch.

Understanding check

Ask: "Match each body to its cargo." "Why the stretch?" "What did YOUR designed car carry?" — cargo, reason, design: the family understood.

This lesson pairs with the Van, Minibus, Limousine & Convertible flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Bulldozer, Excavator, Crane & Forklift — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the building site’s heart: four machines, four verbs — push, dig, lift, carry — acted out with cushions, spoons and rope before ever watching the real thing.

What is this?

Four site machines: bulldozer (push), excavator (dig), crane (lift high) and forklift (carry pallets, beep in reverse).

What does it mean?

Verbs are the deep structure of the construction cards: every machine in the eleven construction spotter sheets does one of these four things, fancier. Learn the verbs once and the whole construction shelf reads itself.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and acting space: a cushion to push, a spoon to dig, a rope-chair "crane" (grown-up power), a box to carry. Then the site visit — from a safe distance.

Why this matters

Acting the verbs builds the category; watching the real machines names it. Order matters: act first, watch second, and the site suddenly makes sense.

What it teaches

Verb vocabulary (push, dig, lift, carry), gross motor imitation, machine-to-verb mapping, and safe-distance observation habits.

Words to learn

bulldozerexcavatorcraneforkliftpushdigliftcarry

Say this to your child

“"Bulldozer PUSHES! Excavator DIGS! Crane LIFTS! Forklift CARRIES — beep, beep, backwards! Four machines, four verbs. Act them with me… now watch a real site: WHO is pushing? WHO is digging? Every machine does a verb!"”

Step by step

  1. Four machines, four verbs: "bulldozer PUSHES… excavator DIGS… crane LIFTS… forklift CARRIES."
  2. Act each: push the cushion, dig with the spoon, lift teddy high (grown-up crane), carry the box with a beep-beep reverse.
  3. The verb hunt on the card: point at each machine, call its verb — fast rounds, big voices.
  4. The site visit: watch a real site from across the road. "Who is pushing? Who is lifting?" The verbs land on steel.
  5. The bridge: "there are ELEVEN more construction cards in this class — all of them push, dig, lift or carry, somehow. Watch for it!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a bulldozer, an excavator with its digging arm, a tower crane and a forklift with its pallet — the site’s four verbs, drawn working.

Ask your child

"Match each machine to its verb." "Which one beeps backwards?" "What did the crane lift on the real site?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might verb every machine on the road ("that one CARRIES!"), act the full site at bedtime, or explain sites to grandparents — verbs, welded to wheels.

Out in the real world

Every town has a site somewhere: fencing, mud, machines. One watched minute from safety teaches more verbs than a week of flashcards.

Try it together

Living-Room Site: cushions = soil, spoon = excavator arm, your arm = crane, shoebox = pallet. Run a full "job" — clear, dig, lift, deliver. Break for beep-beep tea.

Understanding check

Ask: "The four verbs?" (push, dig, lift, carry) "Match each machine." "What did the real crane lift?" — verbs first, machines second: the site reads itself.

This lesson pairs with the Bulldozer, Excavator, Crane & Forklift flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Horse Cart, Sleigh, Wagon & Handcart — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the carts that came before engines: a horse pulling, a sleigh sliding, a wagon rolling, hands pushing — the whole history of transport in four pictures.

What is this?

Four pre-engine movers: horse-drawn carriage, snow sleigh, wooden wagon and handcart — animal power, slide power and muscle power.

What does it mean?

Old-tech cards make new-tech cards make sense: engines are NEW. Before them, the world moved on animals, runners and arms — and all three still work.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the pull-vs-push experiment: a box of toys pulled on a blanket (wagon) vs pushed (handcart) — which is easier? Why?

Why this matters

Children assume the world was always motorized. The sleigh’s runners — wheels that fail on snow, slides that win — is the kind of exception that builds real understanding.

What it teaches

Historical sequencing (then/now), the wheels-vs-runners exception, pull-vs-push physics, and the animal-power category (still alive!).

Words to learn

horse cartsleighwagonhandcartpullpushrunners

Say this to your child

“"Horse cart — clip clop, the horse pulls! Sleigh — swoosh, runners on snow! Wagon — roll, roll. Handcart — push, push! Before engines, the world moved on animals, slides and muscles. Pull the box… now push it — which is easier? THAT is why the horse goes in front!"”

Step by step

  1. Four old movers: "horse cart — the horse PULLS. Sleigh — it SLIDES on snow. Wagon — four wheels, roll. Handcart — YOUR arms push."
  2. The time question: "engines are about a hundred years old. Before that… how did things MOVE?" — these four are the answer.
  3. The experiment: pull the toy-box on a blanket, then push it — "which was easier? Pulling! That is why the horse walks IN FRONT."
  4. The snow exception: "why does the sleigh have NO wheels? Snow swallows wheels — but slides? Swoosh! Runners beat wheels on snow."
  5. The now-hunt: horse carts still work in some towns, wagons haul on farms, handcarts stack every market. Old tech, still employed.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a horse-drawn carriage, a red sleigh, a wooden wagon and a handcart — the pre-engine fleet, still proud.

Ask your child

"Who pulled the cart before engines?" "Why no wheels on the sleigh?" (snow!) "Which was easier — pull or push?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might pull siblings on blankets (wagon service), explain sleighs to a confused snowman, or point out every horse cart in town — history, rolling.

Out in the real world

Living history is findable: carriage rides in old towns, farm wagons, the market handcart. One sighting beats four explanations.

Try it together

Blanket Wagon: pull a loaded blanket across the room, then push the same load — time both. The verdict explains the horse’s position and the cart’s whole design.

Understanding check

Ask: "How did things move before engines?" "Why runners on the sleigh?" "Pull or push — which won?" — then, why, experiment: history earned.

This lesson pairs with the Horse Cart, Sleigh, Wagon & Handcart flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Metro Train, Monorail, Funicular & Steam Locomotive — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the rail family by direction: one runs UNDER the city, one ON a single beam, one UP a mountain on a rope — and one puffs across a hundred years.

What is this?

Four rail rides: metro train (underground), monorail (single elevated beam), funicular (cable-hauled up steep slopes) and steam locomotive (the smoking ancestor).

What does it mean?

Rails are wheels that cannot wander — and each of these four chose a different direction to solve the same problem. Plus the history pair: steam THEN, metro NOW.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the direction sort: under, above, up, across. The steam question — "what made the puff?" — opens the then-and-now conversation.

Why this matters

Trains are the clearest time machine in transport: same rails, different centuries. Children who can order steam-to-metro can order anything.

What it teaches

Direction vocabulary (under, above, up), rail-category thinking, then/now sequencing, and the smoke-to-electric change story.

Words to learn

metromonorailfunicularsteam locomotiveundergroundbeamsteam

Say this to your child

“"Metro train — under the ground, whoosh! Monorail — one beam, up high! Funicular — the rope pulls it UP the mountain. Steam locomotive — CHOO CHOO, puff puff, the grandmother of them all! Same rails — four directions. Which would you ride first?"”

Step by step

  1. Four rails: "metro — UNDER the city! Monorail — ON one beam, up high. Funicular — pulled UP the mountain by a rope. Steam locomotive — CHOO CHOO, with real smoke!"
  2. The direction sort: "under… above… up… across. Same family — four directions!"
  3. The then-and-now: "the steam train is the grandmother of all of them — a hundred years older than the metro. What changed? Smoke out, electricity in."
  4. The ride poll: which rail ride would you take first? (The metro’s under-ground arrival is a favourite.)
  5. The track hunt: rails, beams, the funicular’s cable — find one line that cannot wander.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a metro train, a monorail on its beam, a mountain funicular and a steam locomotive — the rail family, four directions.

Ask your child

"Which one runs UNDER?" "Which climbs a mountain?" (the funicular!) "Which is the oldest?" (steam!) "What changed?" (smoke out, electricity in)

What your child can say or do

Your child might describe metro escalators in detail, spot monorail beams on holiday, or choo-choo with authentic smoke noises — rails, mapped.

Out in the real world

Rail rides are bookable: one metro trip, one heritage steam line, one hill funicular — a year of rail, three tickets. Grandparents optional but excellent.

Try it together

Direction Sort: toy trains vs drawn cards — sort by direction: under (metro mat), over (block beam), up (ramp + string), across (floor). The floor becomes the whole family.

Understanding check

Ask: "Order the four by direction." "Which is oldest?" "What changed from steam to metro?" — directions, history, change: the family complete.

This lesson pairs with the Metro Train, Monorail, Funicular & Steam Locomotive flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Go-Kart, Dune Buggy, Snowmobile & Quad Bike — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the adventure four by their playgrounds: the track kart, the sand buggy, the snow sled and the trail quad — shape follows terrain.

What is this?

Four terrain machines: go-kart (smooth track), dune buggy (sand), snowmobile (snow — runners, not wheels!) and quad bike (any trail four chunky wheels can grip).

What does it mean?

This is terrain-matching: each machine is the answer to one ground. The snowmobile’s missing wheels (runners beat wheels on snow — see the sleigh!) is the card’s best link.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the match: track→kart, sand→buggy, snow→snowmobile, trail→quad. The helmet rule rides with all four.

Why this matters

Terrain-matching is a thinking pattern: the ground writes the machine. Children who see it here will see it in skis, boats and shoes.

What it teaches

Terrain vocabulary (track, sand, snow, trail), machine-to-ground matching, the wheels-vs-runners echo, and helmet-habit reinforcement.

Words to learn

go-kartdune buggysnowmobilequad biketracksandsnowtrail

Say this to your child

“"Go-kart zips the TRACK! Dune buggy jumps the SAND! Snowmobile — vrrroom — slides the SNOW, no wheels, just runners! Quad bike grips the TRAIL. The ground built each machine — and every rider wears a helmet!"”

Step by step

  1. Four machines, four playgrounds: "go-kart — the smooth TRACK. Dune buggy — the SAND. Snowmobile — the SNOW. Quad bike — any TRAIL!"
  2. The snow echo: "wait — where are the snowmobile’s WHEELS? Gone! Remember the sleigh? Runners beat wheels on snow. Same trick, engine-powered."
  3. The match game: call a terrain, the child calls the machine — fast rounds.
  4. The helmet line: "every rider on this card wears a helmet. Even on sand. Especially on sand."
  5. The spot: quads and buggies turn up at farms and beaches — terrain machines are findable.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a go-kart, a dune buggy, a blue snowmobile and a quad bike — four machines, four terrains.

Ask your child

"Match machine to terrain." "Why no wheels on the snowmobile?" "What do all four riders wear?" (helmets!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might match machines to beaches and snowfields on holiday, or remind the family about helmets at the sand dunes — terrain thinking, riding along.

Out in the real world

Farms run quads, dunes host buggies, ski fields buzz with snowmobiles, and every fun fair has a kart track. Terrains are findable.

Try it together

Terrain Sort: draw four grounds, four machines on cards — match at speed. Add the sleigh card for the snow double-up: runners, twice!

Understanding check

Ask: "Match the four to their grounds." "Why runners on snow?" "What does every rider wear?" — terrain, exception, helmet: the adventure four, complete.

This lesson pairs with the Go-Kart, Dune Buggy, Snowmobile & Quad Bike flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Tractor, Combine Harvester, Road Train & Articulated Bus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the longest vehicles in the set: a tractor, a wheat-eating combine, a three-trailer road train and a bus that bends in the middle — plus the fold-test that explains them all.

What is this?

Four long machines: farm tractor, combine harvester, Australian road train (one truck, three trailers) and articulated (bending) bus.

What does it mean?

BIG is the theme, BEND is the secret: a vehicle too long to turn must bend. "Articulated" is a wonderful word that means exactly that — and a paper fold proves it in ten seconds.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, paper and tape for the fold-test, and the Australia story: huge empty roads, one truck doing the work of three.

Why this matters

The bend explains both the bus and the road train — one idea, two giants. The combine’s triple job (reap, thresh, blow straw) is the farm’s greatest machine in one pass.

What it teaches

Length comparison and ordering, the articulation concept, paper-craft proof, and the geography of the road train (big skies, empty roads).

Words to learn

tractorcombine harvesterroad trainarticulatedbendtrailers

Say this to your child

“"Tractor! Combine harvester — chomp, chomp, the wheat is lunch! Road train — one truck, THREE trailers, crossing Australia! Articulated bus — it BENDS in the middle to turn corners! Long, longer, LONGEST — and the bendy ones fold. Watch: paper bus… turn… it bends!"”

Step by step

  1. Four giants: "tractor — pulls everything. Combine — eats whole fields of wheat! Road train — ONE truck, THREE trailers. Articulated bus — bends in the middle!"
  2. The length order: line them up long to longest on the card.
  3. The fold-test: tape two paper cars with a folded hinge — "now turn the corner… IT BENDS! That is what ARTICULATED means."
  4. The Australia story: "the road train crosses huge empty roads — one truck, three trailers, one long haul."
  5. The combine count: "it reaps the wheat, threshes the grain AND blows the straw out — three jobs, one pass!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a blue tractor, an orange combine harvester, a triple-trailer road train and a bending articulated bus — the long-haul giants.

Ask your child

"Order them by length." "What does articulated mean?" (bends in the middle) "How many trailers on the road train?" (three!) "What three jobs does the combine do?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might fold-paper-bend every long vehicle, count road-train trailers on documentaries, or explain combines at harvest time — giants, handled.

Out in the real world

Harvest season runs combines past every country road; articulated buses bend through every city; road trains haul across Australia’s outback highways.

Try it together

Paper Articulation: build a three-trailer paper road train with taped hinges, then navigate the sofa. Corners demand bends — the concept proves itself.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which is longest?" "What does the bend do?" (turns corners) "Name the three-in-one machine." (combine!) — length, bend, jobs: giants understood.

This lesson pairs with the Tractor, Combine Harvester, Road Train & Articulated Bus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Coach Bus, School Bus, Double-Decker Bus & Electric Bus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bus family: the long-distance coach, the yellow school run, the two-floor double-decker and the humming electric — four buses, one bell, endless pretend.

What is this?

Four buses: coach (long journeys), school bus (the morning run), double-decker (two floors, six wheels, London’s signature) and electric bus (quiet, no roar).

What does it mean?

Buses are shared rides — the theme’s community heart. The family shows one machine wearing four jobs, and the electric bus adds the future: quiet streets are being built right now.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the job sort: far journeys, school run, two floors, quiet streets. The wheel count (six on a double-decker!) and the bell are the games.

Why this matters

The school bus is personal for most children; the double-decker is exotic; the electric bus is the future arriving. One family, three tenses — past habit, present ride, future street.

What it teaches

Shared-transport vocabulary, job matching, six-wheel counting, sound comparison (roar vs hum), and ticket-punch pretend play.

Words to learn

coachschool busdouble-deckerelectric busfloorsquietbell

Say this to your child

“"Coach — far away! School bus — to school, every morning! Double-decker — two floors, six wheels, climb the stairs! Electric bus — shhh, it HUMS. Ding — stop please! Four buses, one family. Which one is YOUR ride?"”

Step by step

  1. Four buses: "coach — goes FAR. School bus — brings US to school. Double-decker — TWO floors, climb the stairs! Electric bus — shhh… no engine roar."
  2. The job sort: "who rides the coach? Holiday-makers! The school bus? US!"
  3. The wheel count: "a double-decker needs SIX wheels to carry two floors of people — count them!"
  4. The sound test: "old buses roar. Electric buses HUM — like a fridge with seats. Which street would you rather live on?"
  5. The pretend: chairs in a row, tickets punched, the bell — "stop please!" The family, driven.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a coach bus, a yellow school bus, a red double-decker and a green electric bus — the bus family, four jobs.

Ask your child

"Match each bus to its job." "How many wheels on the double-decker?" (six!) "Which bus is quietest?" (electric — it hums!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might punch tickets for the whole family, count double-decker wheels on screen, or hum their own electric bus — the family, running routes.

Out in the real world

Buses pass every school gate: the yellow run, the city hum, the coach to the museum. One week of watching meets the whole family.

Try it together

Bus Route: chairs, tickets, a bell (any ding), stops named after family members. The driver rotates; the double-decker has stairs (cushion). Fares: one hug.

Understanding check

Ask: "Match the four buses to their jobs." "Count the double-decker’s wheels." "Which is quiet?" — jobs, wheels, hum: the family on route.

This lesson pairs with the Coach Bus, School Bus, Double-Decker Bus & Electric Bus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Race Car, Rally Car, Go-Kart Trailer & Armored Vehicle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the speed-and-shield card: the race car is fast because it is sleek, the armored vehicle is strong because it is thick — two different answers to two different jobs.

What is this?

Four machines: race car (track speed), rally car (gravel jumps), go-kart trailer (the little racer’s ride to the track) and armored vehicle (protection first).

What does it mean?

Fast and strong are two different superpowers: sleek wins races, thickness wins survival. Children who can explain WHY each is shaped its way are doing design reasoning at the highest level.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the shape question: "why is the race car LOW and POINTY? Why is the armored vehicle THICK and HEAVY?" The go-kart trailer is the support-crew story.

Why this matters

Contrast cards teach best in pairs: speed explains sleek, danger explains armor. Both explain why YOUR family car looks like neither — it has a different job.

What it teaches

Design-reasoning contrast, speed/safety vocabulary, the support-crew idea (even racers travel with help), and slow-vs-fast play scenarios.

Words to learn

race carrally cargo-kart trailerarmored vehiclefaststrongprotect

Say this to your child

“"Race car — fast and pointy, zoom! Rally car — jumps the bumps! Armored vehicle — thick and strong, slow and safe. Fast is ONE superpower… strong is the OTHER. And even the go-kart brings its own trailer — every racer has a crew!"”

Step by step

  1. The speed pair: "race car — LOW and pointy, built for the track! Rally car — jumps gravel roads, bumps and all!"
  2. The shield: "armored vehicle — a car in a suit of armor. Thick, heavy, SLOW. Why? Its job is protection, not speed."
  3. The shape question: "fast needs sleek… safe needs thick. TWO superpowers — which does YOUR family car choose?" (Neither extreme — its job is carrying US!)
  4. The crew story: "even the little go-kart travels with its own trailer — every racer has a support crew."
  5. The slow-safe game: armored-vehicle walk (slow, steady, strong) vs race-car sprint (fast!) — act both superpowers.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Land" sits over a low race car, a rally car mid-stride, a go-kart on its trailer and a blue armored vehicle — speed and shield, side by side.

Ask your child

"Why is the race car pointy?" "Why is the armored vehicle slow?" (its job is protection!) "What are the two superpowers?" (fast and strong!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sort every car by superpower, build armored shoebox vehicles, or slow-march like an armored convoy — design reasoning, at play.

Out in the real world

Race weekends, rally clips and armored convoys on the news — fast and strong are on screen weekly. Name the superpower each time one passes.

Try it together

Superpower Sort: toy vehicles into FAST pile and STRONG pile — then design a vehicle with BOTH (the argument is the lesson). Vote on the winner.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the two superpowers." "Match each vehicle to its power." "Why does the armored one move slowly?" — speed, shield, reason: contrast complete.

This lesson pairs with the Race Car, Rally Car, Go-Kart Trailer & Armored Vehicle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Boat, Ship, Sailboat & Submarine — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the water cards with the floating four: boat and ship ride the surface, the sailboat borrows the wind, and the submarine dives under and vanishes.

What is this?

Four water vehicles: boat (small, general), ship (big, ocean), sailboat (wind-powered) and submarine (dives and hides).

What does it mean?

Water vehicles travel on no roads at all — the whole surface is the highway. The submarine is the set’s only vehicle that HIDES, and the sailboat is the only one powered by weather.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a basin or bath, floating and sinking toys, a paper sailboat and breath. The lab runs itself.

Why this matters

Float-or-sink is most children’s first science experiment — and this card turns bath night into the lab. Wind-power is the second lesson: weather can drive a vehicle.

What it teaches

Surface vs underwater thinking, wind-power introduction, float-sink experimentation, and size scaling (boat → ship).

Words to learn

boatshipsailboatsubmarinefloatsinkwinddive

Say this to your child

“"Boat! Ship! Sailboat! Submarine! The boat floats, the ship crosses oceans, the wind pushes the sailboat — whoosh — and the submarine dives down, down, UNDER. Float the toys… blow the sail… dive the submarine. Water transport!"”

Step by step

  1. Four floaters: "boat — small and handy. Ship — BIG, crosses oceans. Sailboat — the wind pushes it! Submarine — dives UNDER the water. Glub glub."
  2. The bath lab: float the toys — "which FLOAT like a boat? Which SINK like… a submarine diving?" Sort and re-sort.
  3. The wind test: paper sailboat, one strong blow — "the WIND moved it! That is how a sailboat works — weather power!"
  4. The dive: duck the submarine toy under — periscope up! "The submarine is the only one that HIDES."
  5. The size ladder: "a boat fits on a trailer. A ship needs a harbour. Same idea — different sizes."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Water" sits over a small boat, a big ship, a sailboat with white sails and a round blue submarine — the floating four, drawn afloat.

Ask your child

"Which one dives?" (the submarine!) "What pushes the sailboat?" (the wind!) "Which is biggest?" (the ship) "Which toys floated?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might run the float lab nightly, blow boats across every puddle, or dive toys with periscope sounds — water vocabulary, afloat.

Out in the real world

Harbours, lakes and the bath: boats dock everywhere. Ferry rides, sail sightings and submarine museums are all bookable water lessons.

Try it together

Harbour Sort: bath toys by water type — surface fleet (boats, ships), wind fleet (sails), dive fleet (submarine). Three fleets, one harbour, one captain.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the floating four." "What powers the sailboat?" (wind) "Which one hides?" (submarine!) — surface, wind, dive: water opened.

This lesson pairs with the Boat, Ship, Sailboat & Submarine flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Ferry, Kayak, Canoe & Speedboat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the river runners: the patient ferry, the double-blade kayak, the single-paddle canoe and the roaring speedboat — with the paddle puzzle at the centre.

What is this?

Four river vehicles: ferry (back and forth, all day), kayak (double-blade paddle), canoe (single paddle, swapped sides) and speedboat (engine power).

What does it mean?

The kayak-canoe pair is a fine paddling puzzle: two blades or one, and WHY one-sided paddling spins you in circles. The spin IS the steering lesson — physics you can act in a chair.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and chair-boats: a stick for a double "kayak" paddle, then a single "canoe" paddle. The spin experiment is the lesson’s heart.

Why this matters

One-side-only paddling spinning the boat is real physics, actable in ten seconds — and it explains why canoeists swap sides. Experiments that explain steering beat rules about steering.

What it teaches

Paddle mechanics, the spin-and-correct experiment, patient-route vocabulary (the ferry), and engine-vs-paddle power categories.

Words to learn

ferrykayakcanoespeedboatpaddlebladespinsteer

Say this to your child

“"Ferry — back and forth, all day! Kayak — two blades, splash splash! Canoe — one paddle… whoa, SPINNING! Swap sides — left, right — straight again! Speedboat — ZOOM! Rivers were the first roads, and these four still run them."”

Step by step

  1. Four river runners: "ferry — back and forth, all day, horn and all. Kayak — TWO blades! Canoe — ONE paddle, swap sides! Speedboat — ZOOM, engine power."
  2. The kayak paddle: chair-boat, double stick — "splash left… splash right… straight ahead!"
  3. The spin experiment: single paddle, ONE side only — "we’re going in a CIRCLE! That is why canoeists swap sides — left, right, left!"
  4. The ferry story: "the ferry is the water’s bus — same crossing, every day, carrying everyone."
  5. The power sort: paddles (kayak, canoe) vs engines (speedboat) vs schedule (ferry). Three powers, four boats.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Water" sits over a ferry, a yellow kayak with its double paddle, a canoe and a speedboat — river runners, four powers.

Ask your child

"Which paddle has two blades?" "Why does one-side paddling spin you?" "What is the water’s bus?" (the ferry!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might chair-paddle through the house, demand side-swaps mid-"canoe," or narrate every ferry crossing — the spin, understood.

Out in the real world

River towns run ferries; lakes rent kayaks and canoes; speedboats sketch across every bay. One river crossing is a term of lessons.

Try it together

Spin Test: office chair or cushion-scoot, one-arm paddles only — spin! Then two-arm: straight. The physics of steering, demonstrated by the captain.

Understanding check

Ask: "Two blades or one — who has which?" "Why swap sides?" (else you spin!) "Who crosses all day?" (the ferry) — paddles, spin, patience: rivers run.

This lesson pairs with the Ferry, Kayak, Canoe & Speedboat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Yacht, Catamaran, Cruise Ship & Lifeboat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ocean fleet: the sailing yacht, the two-hulled catamaran, the cruise ship that is a floating town — and the lifeboat, whose brave job rescues people.

What is this?

Four ocean vehicles: yacht (sailing for joy), catamaran (two hulls — stability!), cruise ship (a thousand rooms) and lifeboat (the rescue specialist).

What does it mean?

The catamaran’s two-hull trick is real engineering a child can test with cups; the lifeboat connects water to the helpers theme; the cruise ship answers "how many people fit on a boat?" like a magic trick.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, two cups taped together (the catamaran test), and the lifeboat story told with respect: crews launch in storms to save others.

Why this matters

Testing stability (one hull vs two) is engineering with household equipment — and the lifeboat gives the ocean fleet its heart: boats have jobs, and the bravest one wears orange.

What it teaches

Stability experimentation, scale wonder (the cruise ship), helper-boat vocabulary, and hull counting that doubles as engineering talk.

Words to learn

yachtcatamaranhullcruise shiplifeboatrescuebrave

Say this to your child

“"Yacht — sailing on the wind! Catamaran — TWO hulls, steady as a table — test it with cups! Cruise ship — a whole town afloat, a thousand rooms! And the lifeboat — brave crews, storm weather, rescuing people. What a fleet!"”

Step by step

  1. The fleet: "yacht — sailing for the joy of it! Catamaran — TWO hulls! Cruise ship — a floating TOWN. Lifeboat — the rescuer."
  2. The hull test: float one cup (wobbly!) vs two taped cups (steady!) — "TWO hulls = steadier. That is the catamaran’s secret!"
  3. The scale question: "how many people fit on a cruise ship? THOUSANDS — pools, theatres, a whole town that floats."
  4. The hero: "the lifeboat launches in STORMS to save ships in trouble. The bravest job on the water."
  5. The fleet review: sail power, stability, scale, rescue — four boats, four ideas.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Water" sits over a white yacht, a two-hulled catamaran, a grand cruise ship and an orange lifeboat — the ocean fleet at anchor.

Ask your child

"How many hulls on a catamaran?" (two!) "Was the two-cup boat steadier?" "What does the lifeboat do?" (rescues!) "How many people fit on a cruise ship?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might tape-cup-test every floating toy, count cruise-ship decks on screen, or salute passing lifeboat stations — the fleet, admired.

Out in the real world

Marinas hold yachts and catamarans, ports berth cruise giants, and every coast keeps its lifeboat station. The fleet is visitable.

Try it together

Cup Fleet: build one-hull and two-hull boats, load "cargo" (coins) — which carries more before tipping? Stability and capacity, tested by the harbourmaster.

Understanding check

Ask: "Why two hulls?" (steadier!) "What floats like a town?" (the cruise ship) "Who launches in storms?" (the lifeboat crews!) — stability, scale, bravery: the fleet sails.

This lesson pairs with the Yacht, Catamaran, Cruise Ship & Lifeboat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Tugboat, Dredger, Hydrofoil & Paddle Steamer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the harbor’s specialists: the tiny tug that moves giants, the dredger that eats mud, the hydrofoil that flies on stilts and the paddle steamer walking on water wheels.

What is this?

Four specialist boats: tugboat (pushes ships many times its size), dredger (digs the bottom), hydrofoil (lifts onto wings and flies) and paddle steamer (the wheeling ancestor).

What does it mean?

Specialists break the rules children just learned: small can move big (tug), boats can fly (hydrofoil), wheels work in water (paddle steamer). Exceptions are where understanding deepens.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a small toy and a big book for the tug test, and the David-and-Goliath framing: tiny boat, giant ship, slow and mighty.

Why this matters

The tug test — can small push big? — is physics, character education and the best story in the water set at once. The hydrofoil bridges straight to the Air cards.

What it teaches

Force intuition (small, steady, mighty), exception thinking, the boat-that-flies bridge, and historical wheel power (the steamer).

Words to learn

tugboatdredgerhydrofoilpaddle steamerpushwingswheels

Say this to your child

“"Tugboat — toot! Small but mighty: it PUSHES the giant ship! Dredger — schlurp, eating the harbour mud. Hydrofoil — up on its wings, FLYING over the water! Paddle steamer — round and round on its wheels, the oldest dance on the river. Harbor specialists!"”

Step by step

  1. The specialists: "tugboat — tiny but MIGHTY. Dredger — eats the mud so ships can park. Hydrofoil — grows wings and FLIES over water! Paddle steamer — walks on its own water wheels."
  2. The tug test: small toy against a big book across the table — "slowly… steadily… IT MOVES! That is a tugboat’s whole job."
  3. The flyer question: "why would a boat want to LIFT out of the water?" — less splash, more speed. The hydrofoil is a boat doing an airplane’s trick.
  4. The wheels: "the paddle steamer walks on wheels — the steam train’s river cousin, from the same century."
  5. The mud story: "harbours fill with mud. The dredger vacuums it out — or the ships run aground. The least glamorous boat, the most necessary."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Water" sits over a blue tugboat, a working dredger, a hydrofoil up on its foils and a paddle steamer mid-wheel — specialists, hard at it.

Ask your child

"Who pushes the giant ships?" (the tugboat!) "What eats the mud?" (the dredger) "Which boat flies?" (the hydrofoil!) "Which walks on wheels?" (the paddle steamer)

What your child can say or do

Your child might tug-test every household object, report dredgers on documentaries, or wheel-walk their arms like a steamer — exceptions, loved.

Out in the real world

Harbours employ all four: tugs escort ships in, dredgers keep channels deep, hydrofoils ferry passengers, and paddle steamers chuff on heritage rivers.

Try it together

Tug Convoy: the small toy "tugs" the cushion-ship across the rug — slow, steady, docking achieved. Add the hydrofoil hand-flight for the finale.

Understanding check

Ask: "Small pushes big — who?" (the tugboat) "Which boat flies?" (hydrofoil) "Whose wheels walk the water?" (paddle steamer) — push, fly, wheel: specialists complete.

This lesson pairs with the Tugboat, Dredger, Hydrofoil & Paddle Steamer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Airplane, Helicopter, Hot-Air Balloon & Rocket — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the sky with its famous four: wings, spinning blades, drifting breeze and the rocket that leaves the whole sky behind — ending, inevitably, in a countdown.

What is this?

Four flyers: airplane (winged), helicopter (rotor-bladed), hot-air balloon (lighter-than-air drift) and rocket (the only vehicle that leaves the planet).

What does it mean?

The sky’s front door: these four are nameable by age three, which makes them the anchor set for every air card after. The rocket’s countdown is also the best transition device in early years.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a paper airplane, a spinning-hand "helicopter," a drawn balloon and the countdown: five-four-three-two-one, blast off, arms up.

Why this matters

Flying is the most wondered-about kind of going. Anchoring wonder on four friendly names turns every contrail into a vocabulary moment.

What it teaches

Air-vehicle vocabulary, glide observation, rotor imitation, countdown sequencing, and the sky-as-a-place category.

Words to learn

airplanehelicopterhot-air balloonrocketflywingsblast off

Say this to your child

“"Airplane! Helicopter! Hot-air balloon! Rocket! Wings, whirring blades, drifting bubbles and… 5-4-3-2-1… BLAST OFF! The rocket is the only one that leaves the whole sky behind. Fly the fleet with me!"”

Step by step

  1. Four flyers: "airplane — big wings! Helicopter — whir-whir-whir on top! Hot-air balloon — floats like a giant bubble. Rocket — 5-4-3-2-1, BLAST OFF!"
  2. The glide test: throw the paper airplane — "wings at work! How far did it fly?"
  3. The rotor: spin one hand over the head — "helicopter blades!" Walk-and-whirr across the room.
  4. The drift: arms wide, sway slowly — "the balloon goes where the wind says. No hurry."
  5. THE COUNTDOWN: five-four-three-two-one… BLAST OFF — everyone crouches, counts, explodes upward. Repeat on request forever.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Air" sits over four labeled flyers: a blue airplane, a helicopter, a striped hot-air balloon and a rocket — the sky’s famous four.

Ask your child

"Which one spins on top?" (helicopter) "Which one floats?" (balloon) "Which leaves the planet?" (rocket!) "Show me the countdown!"

What your child can say or do

Your child might blast off at every opportunity, whirr through hallways, or spot contrails as "airplane lines" — the sky, colonised.

Out in the real world

The sky serves daily: contrails overhead, helicopters over the city, festival balloons, and rocket launches on every screen. Flyovers are free field trips.

Try it together

Airshow: paper planes (glide), hand rotors (hover), balloon arms (drift) and the group countdown (blast off). Four events, one airshow, infinite encores.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the sky’s four." "What spins on a helicopter?" "Show me the countdown!" — wings, blades, breeze, blast-off: the sky is open.

This lesson pairs with the Airplane, Helicopter, Hot-Air Balloon & Rocket flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Jet, Seaplane, Glider & Blimp — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson stretches "airplane" into a family: the jet that outruns sound, the seaplane that parks on lakes, the glider that flies on silence and the blimp that is in no hurry at all.

What is this?

Four air vehicles: jet (fast, high), seaplane (water landings), glider (no engine — wind only) and blimp (floating giant, slower than a bicycle).

What does it mean?

One word — flying — covers four different answers: power (jet), place (seaplane), silence (glider) and slowness (blimp). The glider’s trick — wings work without engines — is real physics a paper plane can prove.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a paper "glider" thrown gently: how far can silence travel? The blimp riddle: why so slow? (It floats — it is in no hurry.)

Why this matters

The glider is the card’s physics star and the blimp is its joke — proof that flying does not always mean fast. Contrast teaches the category better than any single example.

What it teaches

Air-category splitting (power/water/silence/float), glide experiments, sound vocabulary (WHOOSH vs shhh), and gentle-throw motor control.

Words to learn

jetseaplanegliderblimpglidefloatsilent

Say this to your child

“"Jet — WHOOSH, faster than sound! Seaplane — splash, lands on the lake! Glider — shhh, riding the wind with no engine at all. Blimp — the world’s slowest flight, and proud of it. Four ways to fly!"”

Step by step

  1. The family: "jet — faster than sound, WHOOSH! Seaplane — lands on LAKES. Glider — no engine, just wind — shhh. Blimp — slow and round, the giant fish of the sky."
  2. The glide test: gentle paper-glider throws — "engine off… how far did SILENCE fly?"
  3. The parking question: "where does a seaplane park? On the lake — no runway needed!"
  4. The blimp riddle: "why is the blimp slowest of all? It FLOATS — flying without hurrying is still flying."
  5. The sound line-up: jet WHOOSH, seaplane splash, glider shhh, blimp… (drumroll of nothing). Four flyers, four sounds.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Air" sits over a blue jet, a seaplane on its pontoons, a white glider and a round blimp — the air family, four answers.

Ask your child

"Which needs no runway?" (seaplane!) "Which has no engine?" (glider) "Which is slowest?" (blimp!) "How far did your glider fly?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might throw whisper-glides on repeat, park toy planes on bath water, or defend the blimp’s honour — the family, split and sorted.

Out in the real world

Airshows display all four: jets scream, seaplanes scoop, gliders circle silently, blimps drift over stadiums. One airshow covers the family.

Try it together

Glide Contest: same paper, different throws — hard (jet!) vs gentle (glider). Chart which went further. The physics argues for gentle, every time.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who lands on water?" "Who flies engineless?" "Who is slowest?" — power, water, silence, float: four ways to fly, sorted.

This lesson pairs with the Jet, Seaplane, Glider & Blimp flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Drone, Fighter Jet, Cargo Plane & Passenger Plane — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the sky as a workplace: the hovering drone, the fast fighter, the parcel-swallowing cargo plane and the passenger plane that carries hundreds over oceans.

What is this?

Four working aircraft: drone (remote-controlled, camera-eyed), fighter jet (fast patrol), cargo plane (freight) and passenger plane (hundreds of travelers).

What does it mean?

The drone is the NEWEST vehicle in the whole set — most grandparents never saw one as children — which makes this card a then-and-now conversation as much as a vocabulary lesson.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the job sort: people, parcels, patrol, pictures. The drone-pilot pretend (one hand flies, one hand works the remote) is the game.

Why this matters

"The sky is a workplace" reframes every plane in the sky as somebody’s job — and jobs are how children organize the world.

What it teaches

Job sorting (people/parcels/patrol/pictures), the newest-vs-oldest timeline, remote-control concept, and the cargo plane’s nose that opens.

Words to learn

dronefighter jetcargo planepassenger planeremotecargopassengers

Say this to your child

“"Drone — hovering, filming, flown from a remote! Fighter jet — WHOOSH, on patrol! Cargo plane — gulp, the parcels go in the nose! Passenger plane — hundreds of travelers, up above the clouds. Today’s sky is a workplace!"”

Step by step

  1. The staff photo: "drone — flies ITSELF, from a remote! Fighter jet — fast patrol. Cargo plane — swallows the PARCELS. Passenger plane — carries HUNDREDS of travelers."
  2. The job sort: "who carries people? Parcels? Who takes the pictures? Who patrols fast?"
  3. The timeline: "the drone is the newest vehicle in this whole class — your grandparents’ childhoods had NONE. What else is new?"
  4. The cargo trick: "the cargo plane’s NOSE opens to swallow the freight — like a pelican!"
  5. The pilot pretend: one hand hovers (the drone), one thumb works buttons (the remote) — land it on the sofa, gently.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Air" sits over a small drone, a grey fighter jet, a giant cargo plane and a passenger jet — the working sky, drawn on duty.

Ask your child

"Who carries people? Parcels?" "Which is the newest?" (the drone!) "What opens on the cargo plane?" (the nose!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might remote-hand drones through doorways, classify every plane at the airport window, or explain drones to amazed elders — the workplace, staffed.

Out in the real world

Airports, drone shots on every nature documentary, cargo giants at the freight terminal — the working sky is visible from any window with patience.

Try it together

Air Traffic Control: paper planes as the fleet — cargo (carries a sticker load), passenger (carries a peg person), drone (hand-launched, hovers). The tower (you) clears each for landing.

Understanding check

Ask: "Sort the four by cargo." "Which vehicle is newest?" "What does a passenger plane carry?" (people — hundreds!) — jobs, timeline, cargo: the sky, employed.

This lesson pairs with the Drone, Fighter Jet, Cargo Plane & Passenger Plane flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Space Shuttle, Hang Glider, Gyrocopter & Flying Boat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches flight’s edges: the shuttle that rode a rocket to orbit and glided home, the hang glider riding breeze like a bird, the gyrocopter’s free-spinning blade and the flying boat that lands like a duck.

What is this?

Four specialists: space shuttle (orbit and back), hang glider (engineless soaring), gyrocopter (unpowered top rotor) and flying boat (a boat with wings).

What does it mean?

Edge-of-flight cards show what flying CAN be: space, silence, simplicity, splashdowns. The shuttle is history now — retired — which makes it a museum conversation as much as a vehicle.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and hang-glider arms: lean, arms wide, glide across the room — the slowest race ever. The space question: which one has been to SPACE?

Why this matters

Specialists each solve one problem — space, silence, smallness, water — and solving-problems-by-design is the deepest idea the air cards can leave.

What it teaches

Edge-category thinking, glide imitation (slow bodies!), the retired-vehicle history note, and the duck-landing bridge back to water-01.

Words to learn

space shuttlehang glidergyrocopterflying boatorbitsoarglide

Say this to your child

“"Space shuttle — to orbit and BACK! Hang glider — arms wide, riding the breeze, slowest race ever. Gyrocopter — its top blade spins free in the wind! Flying boat — lands on the lake like a duck. The specialists of the sky!"”

Step by step

  1. The specialists: "space shuttle — rode a rocket to SPACE, glided home like a plane! Hang glider — hangs under a wing, rides the breeze. Gyrocopter — a blade spins above, free! Flying boat — a boat with wings, lands on water like a duck."
  2. The glide: arms wide, lean, cross the room — "slowest race in the class! That is hang-gliding."
  3. The space question: "which one has been to SPACE? The shuttle — and it retired years ago. Museums keep them now."
  4. The bridge: "the flying boat is two vehicles at once — water-01’s cousin with wings!"
  5. The specialist review: space, breeze, rotor, splash — four edges of the sky.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Air" sits over a space shuttle, a hang glider under its wing, a small gyrocopter and a flying boat — the edges of flight, drawn soaring.

Ask your child

"Which one went to SPACE?" (the shuttle!) "Show me the hang-glider glide!" "Which lands like a duck?" (the flying boat!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might glide the length of the house, demand the space museum, or duck-land every toy plane in the bath — the edges, explored.

Out in the real world

Space museums display real shuttles; hills host hang gliders on windy Sundays; airshows fly gyrocopters; lakeside towns watch flying boats at vintage meets.

Try it together

Edge Certificates: four stations — glide (arms), rotor (hand-spin), splash-land (bath), blast-off (countdown) — earn a sticker per station. Certified specialist of the sky.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the four specialists." "Which one is retired?" (the shuttle — museums!) "Show me the glide!" — space, breeze, rotor, splash: edges complete.

This lesson pairs with the Space Shuttle, Hang Glider, Gyrocopter & Flying Boat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Road Roller, Mixer, Dump Truck & Paver — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the road crew in order: flatten the ground, mix the concrete, dump the gravel, lay the smooth black road — a full road, built on the living-room floor.

What is this?

Four road-building machines: road roller (flatten), concrete mixer (tumbling drum), dump truck (the load) and asphalt paver (the smooth layer behind it).

What does it mean?

This card answers the question every child asks while watching a street get fixed: who does WHAT? Four machines, four steps, one road — a sequence the toys can replay end to end.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a paint roller (the road roller), a spinning jar (mixer), a toy tipper and a rectangular block (paver). Build the road across the rug.

Why this matters

Sequence-building (step one, two, three, four) is the deep skill here — construction is the friendliest place to learn that big jobs are ordered small jobs.

What it teaches

Sequencing (build order), machine-to-step mapping, rolling and tipping motor play, and the road-under-our-feet appreciation.

Words to learn

road rollermixerdump truckpaverflattenlayroad

Say this to your child

“"Road roller — FLAT! Mixer — round and round! Dump truck — CRASH, there is the gravel! Paver — smooth, smooth, the road appears! Four machines, four steps, one brand-new road. Now drive on it — the crew approves!"”

Step by step

  1. The crew in order: "road roller — sllloooow, FLAT. Mixer — round and round. Dump truck — tips the load, CRASH. Paver — lays the road smooth as icing!"
  2. Build it: flatten (roller), mix (jar spin), dump (tipper), lay (block slides forward leaving "road").
  3. The question: "next time a street is dug up — WHO does each step? Watch!"
  4. The roller’s charm: "the roller is a giant rolling pin — for roads instead of cookies."
  5. The road test: drive a toy car along the freshly laid rug-road. The crew inspects its work.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a road roller, a concrete mixer truck, a dump truck and an asphalt paver — the road crew, in build order.

Ask your child

"What does the roller do?" (flattens) "Which machine mixes?" "Which lays the road?" "What are the four steps?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might build roads across every rug, roll toys flat with rolling-pin reverence, or narrate street works like a foreman — the crew, employed.

Out in the real world

Road works hire the whole crew in public: rollers idling, mixers turning, pavers crawling. One ten-minute watch from safety covers the card.

Try it together

Roadworks Replay: the full sequence with toys — flatten, mix, dump, lay, DRIVE. Add a "road closed" sign (paper) for authenticity. Reopen when the crew waves through.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the crew in order." "What flattens?" (roller) "What lays the smooth road?" (paver) — flatten, mix, dump, lay: a road is born.

This lesson pairs with the Road Roller, Mixer, Dump Truck & Paver flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Wheel Loader, Backhoe, Grader & Skid-Steer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the scoop squad: four machines built around moving material — big bites, back arms, flat shaves and one pirouetting dancer.

What is this?

Four loaders: wheel loader (swallows gravel heaps), backhoe loader (a digger riding on a loader’s back), motor grader (shaves ground flat) and skid-steer (tiny, fast, spins on the spot).

What does it mean?

All four exist for one verb — move material — which makes this the set’s cleanest compare-and-contrast: same job, four bodies. The skid-steer’s pirouette is the crowd favourite.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, pom-poms as gravel, a scoop or dustpan, and one leg for the pivot test. The relay does the teaching.

Why this matters

Same-verb-different-body comparison builds real analysis: children stop seeing "diggers" and start seeing four tools for one job — each best at a different corner of it.

What it teaches

Comparative analysis, scoop-and-carry motor control, pivot balance (the skid-steer test), and material-handling vocabulary.

Words to learn

wheel loaderbackhoemotor graderskid-steerscoopgravelspin

Say this to your child

“"Wheel loader — CHOMP, a big bite! Backhoe — digger on a loader’s back, two machines in one! Grader — shave, shave, flat as a pancake. Skid-steer — spin, spin on the spot, the dancer of the site! Four bodies, one job: MOVE IT."”

Step by step

  1. The squad: "wheel loader — one BIG bite of gravel! Backhoe — a digger riding a loader! Grader — shaves the ground flat as a pancake. Skid-steer — the little one that SPINS on the spot!"
  2. The relay: pom-pom gravel moved scoop-ful by scoop-ful — loader style, big bites only.
  3. The backhoe double: "two machines in one — digger behind, loader in front. It does BOTH jobs!"
  4. The pivot: stand on one foot, spin slowly — "a skid-steer pirouette! It turns on a coin, in the mud."
  5. The shave: the grader’s job is the FLAT — "smooth ground is the first step of every building."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a wheel loader, a backhoe loader, a motor grader and a skid-steer — the scoop squad, lined up.

Ask your child

"Which one spins?" (skid-steer!) "Which is two machines in one?" (backhoe) "What does the grader make?" (flat ground) "Move the gravel — how?" (scoop, big bites!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might pivot-spin through the kitchen, scoop-relay every pom-pom in the house, or spot backhoes on every street — the squad, hired.

Out in the real world

Every housing site runs the squad: loaders biting, graders shaving, skid-steers dancing between them. One fence-line view covers the card.

Try it together

Gravel Company: pom-poms mined from one bowl, delivered to another, flat-shaved at the end (the grader’s finish). Full shift, full pride, full nap.

Understanding check

Ask: "The one verb they share?" (move it!) "Who spins?" "Who is two machines?" — squad, verb, spin: compared and known.

This lesson pairs with the Wheel Loader, Backhoe, Grader & Skid-Steer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Drilling Rig, Pile Driver, Telehandler & Boom Lift — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches direction by machine: two go DOWN (drill, hammer), two go UP (telescope arm, basket lift) — and the BAM of the pile driver is the loudest lesson on the card.

What is this?

Four deep-and-high machines: drilling rig (bores down), pile driver (hammers giant nails into the earth), telehandler (telescopes out AND up) and boom lift (carries people in a basket to the sky).

What does it mean?

Foundations are invisible once built — the pile driver’s hammering is one of the few construction acts children get to HEAR. Direction (down/up) gives the card its clean structure.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a spoon "drill," a soft hammer "pile driver," and a tiptoe "telehandler" reach. The BAM question — why hammer giant nails? — is the depth.

Why this matters

Tall buildings need strong grips on the earth: piles are the secret underneath every skyline. Children who know the BAM know what holds the city up.

What it teaches

Direction vocabulary (down, up), sound-to-machine mapping (BAM!), reach measurement (how high?), and the foundations-under-everything idea.

Words to learn

drilling rigpile drivertelehandlerboom liftdrillhammerreachbasket

Say this to your child
