“"Drilling rig — down, down, DOWN! Pile driver — BAM, BAM, giant nails into the earth! Telehandler — out and UP, a telescope arm! Boom lift — a basket to the sky, higher than the trees! Deep and high — that is how cities stand."”

Step by step

  1. Two down, two up: "drilling rig — DOWN, down, down into the ground. Pile driver — BAM, giant nails! Telehandler — OUT and UP, a telescope arm. Boom lift — a BASKET to the sky!"
  2. Act them: spoon-drill the earth (a plant pot), soft-hammer BAM a "pile" (a dowel), tiptoe-reach higher and higher, teddy rides the "basket" (your hands).
  3. The BAM question: "why hammer giant nails into the earth? Tall buildings need strong GRIPS — the piles hold everything up."
  4. The reach record: how high is the real telehandler? Six houses high. Measure your house — multiply!
  5. The site sound: next hammering site, name it from afar: "the pile driver! BAM, BAM — building grips."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a drilling rig, a pile driver mid-BAM, a telehandler with its telescope arm and a boom lift’s raised basket — deep and high, drawn working.

Ask your child

"Which two go DOWN?" (drill, pile driver) "Which go UP?" (telehandler, boom lift) "What does the BAM build?" (grips for tall buildings!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might BAM spoons responsibly, measure reaches against houses, or explain piles from the back seat — direction, engineered.

Out in the real world

City sites drive piles weekly — the BAM carries across whole blocks. Sky platforms (boom lifts) wash every tall window in town.

Try it together

Deep-and-High Course: drill (spoon), BAM (soft hammer), reach (tiptoe record), basket (teddy lifted) — four stations, certified down-and-up operator.

Understanding check

Ask: "Sort the four by direction." "What holds tall buildings up?" (the piles — BAM!) "How high does the boom lift go?" — down, up, why: deep and high.

This lesson pairs with the Drilling Rig, Pile Driver, Telehandler & Boom Lift flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Scissor Lift, Material Lift, Tunnel Borer & Trencher — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches up-and-through: lifts that fold like scissors, the tunnel borer that eats through mountains, and the trencher that draws a straight line in the earth like a giant pencil.

What is this?

Four up-and-through machines: scissor lift (folds upward), material lift (hoists loads up scaffolds), tunnel boring machine (chews tunnels — the set’s biggest vehicle) and trenching machine (cuts long straight ditches).

What does it mean?

The tunnel borer is the biggest machine in the entire class — some as long as a football field — and its cousin is the worm in the apple. Same idea, city scale.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, scissor-hands (open-close like the lift), a blanket "mountain" to crawl through, and chalk for the trencher’s straight line.

Why this matters

Underground construction is invisible in real life — the blanket-tunnel game makes it edible. The scissor-finger mechanism is also a favourite hand exercise.

What it teaches

Mechanism imitation (scissor folding), through-tunnel crawling, straight-line drawing, and the underground-city idea (pipes and trains below!).

Words to learn

scissor liftmaterial lifttunnel boring machinetrencherfoldtunnelditch

Say this to your child

“"Scissor lift — folds UP, like your hands! Material lift — hoist, hoist, up the scaffold! Tunnel borer — CRUNCH through the mountain, the biggest machine in the class! Trencher — draws a straight ditch, a giant pencil. Up, up, THROUGH, and line!"”

Step by step

  1. Up first: "scissor lift — folds UP like scissors! Material lift — hoists loads up the scaffold."
  2. Scissor-hands: open-close, open-close, rising — "that is the lift’s whole secret — folding scissors!"
  3. Through: "the tunnel borer — CRUNCH, CRUNCH — chews a tunnel through a MOUNTAIN. It is the biggest machine in this whole class!"
  4. The blanket mountain: crawl through while a partner chants "crunch, crunch, keep boring!" — the tunnel game.
  5. The line: "the trencher draws a long straight ditch — a giant pencil! Pipes and cables ride in its line."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a scissor lift rising, a material lift at its scaffold, a tunnel borer’s giant face and a trenching machine — up and through.

Ask your child

"What folds like scissors?" (the lift) "What chews tunnels?" (the borer — biggest machine!) "What draws the ditch?" (the trencher — a giant pencil!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might scissor-hand everything upward, blanket-tunnel on demand, or chalk trench-lines down the pavement — up and through, mastered.

Out in the real world

Metro tunnels are bored under most big cities — the machines make the news when they break through. Scissor lifts park at every shopping-centre ceiling repair.

Try it together

The Boring Company: sofa-cushion mountains, blanket tunnels, a crawling crew and a chant. The tunnel opens; the train (the child) drives through; the company declares dividends.

Understanding check

Ask: "What folds up?" (scissor lift) "What chews through mountains?" (the borer!) "What draws straight ditches?" (the trencher) — fold, chew, draw: up and through.

This lesson pairs with the Scissor Lift, Material Lift, Tunnel Borer & Trencher flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Pump Truck, Water Truck, Lowboy & Batching Plant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the quiet heroes: the pump truck pouring concrete through a folding arm like a giant straw, the dust-settling water truck, the flat lowboy carrying giants and the batching plant mixing on the spot.

What is this?

Four support machines: concrete pump truck (long folding arm), water truck (sprinkles dust flat), lowboy trailer (carries the giant machines) and mobile batching plant (mixes concrete on site).

What does it mean?

None of these build anything — and none of the others could build without them. The support-fleet idea is a first lesson in how work really gets done: the crew behind the crew comes first.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a bendy straw (the pump trick), a spray bottle (water truck) and the flat-truck question: "why is the lowboy SO low?"

Why this matters

The straw demo — moving liquid through a long folding arm — makes the pump truck’s genius drinkable. The lowboy answers the highway question: why is that truck so flat? So the giants can climb on.

What it teaches

Support-role thinking, straw-fluid demonstration, sprinkling control, the low-flat-for-loading reason, and on-site mixing logistics.

Words to learn

concrete pumpwater trucklowboybatching plantarmsprinkleflat

Say this to your child

“"Pump truck — slurp, concrete through the giant straw-arm! Water truck — sprinkle, the dust stays down. Lowboy — flat and low, the giants climb aboard! Batching plant — mixing concrete RIGHT THERE. The heroes get the glory — the support fleet makes it possible!"”

Step by step

  1. The fleet: "pump truck — pours concrete through a folding arm, like a giant STRAW! Water truck — sprinkle, sprinkle, the dust stays down. Lowboy — SO flat, it carries the giant machines. Batching plant — mixes concrete RIGHT on the spot."
  2. The straw demo: sip through a long bendy straw — "that is the pump arm: liquid, delivered far away!"
  3. The sprinkle: mist the dusty sandbox — "the water truck’s job: dust down, air clean."
  4. The lowboy question: "why SO low and flat? Ramps! The excavators climb on." (Connect to construction-08’s hauler.)
  5. The support salute: "before the heroes build, the support crew arrives. Power, water, concrete, transport — ALL ready."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a pump truck with its folded arm, a water truck, a flat lowboy trailer and a mobile batching plant — the support fleet, standing by.

Ask your child

"What does the pump arm do?" (pours concrete far away) "Why is the lowboy so low?" (ramps for the giants!) "What does the water truck settle?" (the dust!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might straw-demo every drink, spray-bottle "water-truck" the garden, or load toys onto flat cushions — support thinking, running.

Out in the real world

Every big site hosts the fleet: pump arms reaching second floors, water trucks circling, lowboys delivering diggers at dawn. Dawn deliveries are the best spectating.

Try it together

Support Run: the toys build a "tower" — the straw-arm pours (water into a cup), the spray-bottle settles the dust, the flat cushion delivers the builder. The tower rises on support.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who pours concrete far away?" (the pump truck) "Who carries the giants?" (the lowboy) "Who comes first — heroes or support?" (support!) — arm, sprinkle, flat: the fleet behind the crew.

This lesson pairs with the Pump Truck, Water Truck, Lowboy & Batching Plant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Street Sweeper, Snowplow, Line Painter & Rail Grinder — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the maintainers: the sweeper that brushes, the plow that shoves white waves, the painter that draws the road’s lines and the grinder that showers sparks to keep tracks smooth.

What is this?

Four keeping machines: street sweeper (brushes gutters), snowplow (moves snow), pavement marking machine (paints lines) and rail grinder (sparks — shaves the tracks smooth).

What does it mean?

These machines exist to keep everything ELSE working — a quietly beautiful idea to hand a child: roads need brushing, snow needs pushing, lines need painting. Maintenance is a form of care.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, masking-tape roads and chalk (the line-painting job), and the sparks question: "why does the rail grinder make FIREWORKS?"

Why this matters

The rail grinder’s sparks are the most impressive tidying-up on Earth — and the line-painting job is a genuine fine-motor activity the machine does at walking pace.

What it teaches

Maintenance-as-care thinking, straight-line painting (fine motor), weather-response vocabulary (snow!), and the spark explanation (metal on metal).

Words to learn

street sweepersnowplowline painterrail grinderbrushplowpaintsparks

Say this to your child

“"Street sweeper — brush brush! Snowplow — WHOOSH, the snow moves! Line painter — the long yellow line, drawn slow and straight. Rail grinder — SPARKS, the tracks get a shave! The keepers: roads brushed, snow pushed, lines painted, rails smooth."”

Step by step

  1. The keepers: "sweeper — brush, brush, clean gutters. Snowplow — WHOOSH, mountains of snow move aside! Line painter — the road’s long yellow lines, drawn at walking pace. Rail grinder — SPARKS! The tracks get a shave."
  2. The painting job: tape a road, chalk the centre line — "straight lines are a real skill; the machine does it slowly, so can you."
  3. The sparks question: "grinding metal makes sparks — the track’s bumps get ground smooth, or trains bump and bang."
  4. The weather crew: "when it snows, the plows work ALL NIGHT so the morning can happen."
  5. The thanks: "these machines exist so everything else works. The quietest heroes on the road."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a street sweeper, a snowplow, a pavement marking machine and a rail grinder mid-sparks — the keepers, on shift.

Ask your child

"Who brushes the streets?" "Who pushes the snow?" "What makes the sparks?" (the rail grinder!) "What does the line painter draw?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might chalk perfect road lines, plow snow-piles with toy trucks, or gasp at real rail-grinding sparks — maintenance, admired.

Out in the real world

Sweepers circle at dawn, plows run all night in snow country, line painters close lanes on Sundays, and rail grinders spark at midnight. The keepers keep odd hours.

Try it together

Keeper Shift: sweep the rug (crumbs!), plow the "snow" (paper scraps), tape-and-chalk a road with proper lines, finish with a spark dance. The whole shift, one living room.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the keepers." "Why the sparks?" (grinding metal smooth!) "What would happen with no snowplows?" — brush, plow, paint, sparks: care with wheels.

This lesson pairs with the Street Sweeper, Snowplow, Line Painter & Rail Grinder flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cold Planer, Asphalt Recycler, Curb Machine & Slipform Paver — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the road doctors: the planer that shaves old bumpy surface like a giant cheese grater, the recycler that melts it into NEW road, the curb machine that squeezes out sidewalk edges and the paver that glides fresh lanes into being.

What is this?

Four road-fixing machines: cold planer (shaves old surface), asphalt recycler (melts chewings into new road), curb machine (extrudes the pavement edge) and slipform paver (pours fresh smooth lanes in one glide).

What does it mean?

This card is the construction set’s recycling lesson: old road is not rubbish — it melts and comes back as new road. And the curb machine answers how sidewalks get their raised edge.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, an old crayon and a grater (grown-up hands — the planer demo), and the melt-and-return story for recycling.

Why this matters

"Roads can be born again" is recycling at infrastructure scale — concrete, visible, delicious to explain. The crayon-shaving demo makes the planer’s job sensory.

What it teaches

Recycling thinking at big scale, shave-melt-relay sequencing, the curb question (how DID the sidewalk get its edge?), and glide-pour continuity.

Words to learn

cold planerrecyclercurb machineslipform pavershavemeltcurblane

Say this to your child

“"Cold planer — scrape, the old bumpy road comes OFF! Recycler — melt the shavings into NEW road — roads are born again! Curb machine — squeezes the sidewalk’s edge like icing! Slipform paver — glide, glide, fresh smooth lane behind it. The road doctors!"”

Step by step

  1. The doctors: "cold planer — shaves the old bumpy road, like a giant cheese grater! Recycler — MELTS the shavings into new road! Curb machine — squeezes out the sidewalk’s edge. Slipform paver — glides along, leaving fresh smooth lane!"
  2. The crayon demo: grate an old crayon (grown-up) — "shavings! That is the planer’s job — old surface off."
  3. The recycling: "the shavings are not rubbish — they MELT and come back as brand-new road. Roads are born again!"
  4. The curb question: "how did the sidewalk get its raised edge? A machine SQUEEZES it out, like icing!"
  5. The glide: hand-gliding a block across the table leaving a "lane" — the paver’s one-pass magic.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a cold planer, an asphalt recycler, a curb machine extruding an edge and a slipform paver laying lane — the road doctors, mid-surgery.

Ask your child

"What shaves the old road?" (the planer) "What happens to the shavings?" (melted — NEW road!) "How does the sidewalk get its edge?" (squeezed out!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might grate crayons for science (supervised), explain road-born-again to everyone, or hunt curbs for squeezing evidence — recycling, infrastructure-scale.

Out in the real world

Road resurfacing closes lanes all summer: planers first, recyclers and pavers behind. Watch one resurfacing job and the whole card drives past.

Try it together

Road Hospital: the toy road is "bumpy" (build obstacles) — shave (grate side of a box, gently), recycle (melted crayon art, grown-up iron on paper), re-pave (smooth paper laid). Discharged, good as new.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the planer do?" (shaves) "What happens to old road?" (born again — recycled!) "Who writes curbs?" (the curb machine) — shave, melt, squeeze, glide: roads mended.

This lesson pairs with the Cold Planer, Asphalt Recycler, Curb Machine & Slipform Paver flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Articulated Hauler, Motor Scraper, Pipe Layer & Trench Compactor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the earthmovers: the hauler that bends to carry mountains, the scraper that eats ground into its own belly, the pipe layer threading the water’s secret roads and the compactor stamping the earth firm.

What is this?

Four earthmoving machines: articulated hauler (bends, hauls tons), motor scraper (shaves ground into itself), pipe layer (lowers pipes into trenches) and trench compactor (stamps earth hard).

What does it mean?

The bend-in-the-middle repeat — the same hinge as the articulated bus, doing far harder work. And the pipe layer reveals infrastructure’s secret: beneath every road runs a hidden water city.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, two toy trucks and tape (the bendy-hauler build), and the big question: "where does the tap water come from?"

Why this matters

The invisible city beneath the road — pipes, sewers, cables — is a genuine revelation to children. The pipe layer makes it visible; the compactor explains why the ground must be stamped hard first.

What it teaches

Articulation reuse (bus → hauler), hidden-infrastructure thinking, stamping motor work (compaction!), and shave-into-belly mechanics.

Words to learn

haulermotor scraperpipe layercompactorbendpipesstamp

Say this to your child

“"Hauler — bends in the middle, hauling a MOUNTAIN! Scraper — shaves the ground into its belly! Pipe layer — the water’s secret roads, laid under every street! Compactor — STAMP, stamp, the earth drum-tight. The earthmovers move the world so the world can be built on it."”

Step by step

  1. The crew: "hauler — bends in the MIDDLE, carries a mountain of dirt! Motor scraper — shaves the ground INTO its own belly. Pipe layer — lowers pipes like thread through a needle. Compactor — STAMP, stamp — the earth, hard as a drum."
  2. The bend build: tape two trucks with a paper hinge — "it bends! The same trick as the articulated bus — but hauling MUD."
  3. The secret roads: "under every street run water pipes and sewers — the pipe layer lays them. The water’s secret roads!"
  4. The stamp test: stamp the sandbox with both feet — firm! "Loose ground squishes; stamped ground HOLDS roads up."
  5. The scraper’s trick: "it shaves the ground and KEEPS it — a belly full of earth, delivered downhill."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over an articulated hauler mid-bend, a motor scraper, a pipe layer lowering pipe and a trench compactor — the earthmovers, ground truth.

Ask your child

"What bends on the hauler?" (its middle!) "Where do the pipes go?" (under the roads — secret water roads!) "Why stamp the earth?" (loose ground squishes — firm holds!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might hinge-tape every toy pair, hunt drain covers as "pipe evidence," or stamp-test every sandbox — earthmoving, grounded.

Out in the real world

Every new suburb is earthmovers first: haulers bending, pipes threading, compactors drumming. The secret city is laid before the houses.

Try it together

Pipe Workers: dig a sandbox trench, lay a "pipe" (pool noodle), cover, stamp firm — then "find" it again with a spoon excavator. The hidden city, met twice.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who bends to haul?" (the hauler) "What hides under streets?" (pipes!) "Why stamp?" (firm ground holds) — bend, shave, lay, stamp: the earth obeys.

This lesson pairs with the Articulated Hauler, Motor Scraper, Pipe Layer & Trench Compactor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Vacuum Excavator, Crawler Carrier, Tracked Carrier & Material Handler — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the clever movers: the vacuum that digs without touching, the tank-tread carriers that walk where wheels sink, and the handler whose grab-arm is the world’s biggest claw machine.

What is this?

Four clever machines: vacuum excavator (sucks soil — digs without touching), crawler and tracked carriers (tank treads for soft ground) and material handler (grab-arm pick and place).

What does it mean?

The vacuum excavator is the set’s most surprising machine — digging without touching, so buried pipes stay safe. And the treads answer a nature question: wheels sink in mud; snowshoes and tank treads walk.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a clothes-peg "grabber" and pom-poms (the claw practice), and the tread question: "why TANK FEET instead of wheels?"

Why this matters

Claw-machine pretend is irresistible and it trains exactly the grip the handler uses. The vacuum’s safe-digging idea — look before you dig — is real safety culture, made vivid.

What it teaches

Vacuum/suction concept, tread-vs-wheel physics, peg-grabber fine motor, and the safe-excavation message (call before you dig!).

Words to learn

vacuum excavatorcrawlertracked carriermaterial handlersuctiontreadsgrab

Say this to your child

“"Vacuum excavator — SCHLOOP! It sucks the soil — digging without touching, keeping the pipes safe! Crawlers — tank feet, step step over the mud where wheels would sink. Material handler — grab, lift, PLACE — the biggest claw machine in the world!"”

Step by step

  1. The clever four: "vacuum excavator — SCHLOOP, sucks the soil — digging without touching! Crawler and tracked carriers — TANK FEET, they walk where wheels sink! Material handler — grab, lift, place — the biggest claw machine alive."
  2. The claw practice: clothes-peg pom-pom moves — grab, carry, place on a tower. Handler’s verbs, trained.
  3. The tread question: "why tank feet? In deep mud, WHEELS sink — treads WALK. Nature thought of it first: snowshoes!"
  4. The vacuum’s wisdom: "digging blind can break buried pipes. The vacuum sucks the soil AWAY — the pipes stay safe. Look before you dig!"
  5. The arcade connection: "every claw-machine player knows this machine’s exact joy — and its heartbreak when the grab drops."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a vacuum excavator with its hose, a crawler carrier, a tracked carrier and a material handler mid-grab — clever movers, drawn thinking.

Ask your child

"Who digs WITHOUT touching?" (the vacuum!) "Why tank feet?" (wheels sink — treads walk!) "What does the handler do?" (grab, lift, place!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might peg-grab everything, vacuum-imitate the dustpan, or explain snowshoes via excavators — cleverness, circulating.

Out in the real world

Utility crews vacuum-dig before every street repair (call before you dig!); crawlers haunt bogs and mines; handlers load scrapyards like enormous arcades.

Try it together

Claw Arcade: peg-grab pom-poms onto a tower, timed rounds, heartbreak drops included — then the vacuum round: a straw "sucks" paper scraps from a tray. Both movers, one arcade.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who digs without touching?" (vacuum) "Who walks on tank feet?" (the carriers) "Who plays claw machine for a living?" (the handler!) — suck, walk, grab: cleverness hired.

This lesson pairs with the Vacuum Excavator, Crawler Carrier, Tracked Carrier & Material Handler flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Tower Crane, Crawler Crane, Rough-Terrain Crane & Truck Crane — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the crane family: the skyline giant, the treads-and-tonnage lift, the mud-hopping rough-terrain and the drive-itself truck crane — with the counterweight experiment at the centre.

What is this?

Four cranes: tower crane (the skyline signature), crawler crane (heaviest lifts on treads), rough-terrain crane (jumps mud) and truck-mounted crane (drives to every small job).

What does it mean?

Four cranes, four answers to one question — how do we lift the heaviest things into the sky? The counterweight is the physics heart: a heavy something on the other side keeps the arm honest.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the balance game: hold a book at arm’s length (heavy!), then build a spoon crane with a cup counterweight — lift a pom-pom load.

Why this matters

Tower cranes are the skyline’s signature and children spot them from farther than any other machine. The counterweight experiment turns wonder into mechanics.

What it teaches

Lifting-mechanics thinking (counterweight!), height comparison, terrain-to-crane matching, and arm-hold endurance (the honest way to feel a crane).

Words to learn

tower cranecrawler cranerough-terrain cranetruck craneliftcounterweightload

Say this to your child

“"Tower crane — tallest of all, king of the skyline! Crawler crane — treads and TONNAGE, the heaviest lifts! Rough-terrain crane — hops the mud! Truck crane — drives itself to little jobs. And the secret of every crane: the COUNTERWEIGHT — heavy one side, load flies the other!"”

Step by step

  1. The family: "tower crane — the TALLEST, it watches the whole city! Crawler crane — treads, and the HEAVIEST lifts. Rough-terrain crane — hops the mud. Truck crane — drives itself to every little job."
  2. The height sort: which is tallest? (Tower — often higher than the building it builds!)
  3. The arm test: hold a book at arm’s length — "heavy, right? Cranes do that ALL DAY — with a secret: the COUNTERWEIGHT."
  4. The spoon crane: spoon arm, tape pivot, cup counterweight — "heavy cup one side… pom-pom load lifts easy the other!"
  5. The spot: tower cranes rule every skyline — "count them from the window. Every one is building something."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a tall tower crane, a tracked crawler crane, a rough-terrain crane and a truck-mounted crane — the family, rigged and ready.

Ask your child

"Which crane is tallest?" (tower!) "Which lifts heaviest?" (crawler) "What balances the load?" (the counterweight!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count tower cranes from every window, spoon-crane everything, or explain counterweights at the playground — the family, spotted and understood.

Out in the real world

Skylines are crane calendars: count them and count the construction. Crawler cranes assemble wind turbines; truck cranes fix every rooftop.

Try it together

Crane School: build the spoon crane, lift loads of increasing weight, adjust the counterweight until it balances — then certify the operator. The skyline awaits.

Understanding check

Ask: "Match each crane to its job." "What balances the arm?" (counterweight!) "Which is tallest?" (tower) — family, physics, skyline: lifting, mastered.

This lesson pairs with the Tower Crane, Crawler Crane, Rough-Terrain Crane & Truck Crane flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · TRANSPORTATION & VEHICLES · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Generator, Light Tower, Compressor & Welding Truck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson closes the construction shelf with its quiet heroes: four trailers that bring the electricity, the light, the air and the sparks — and the big idea that support comes first.

What is this?

Four power machines: generator trailer (site electricity), light tower trailer (lamps that turn night into day), compressor trailer (air for the tools) and welding truck (joins steel with sparks).

What does it mean?

None of them build anything — and none of the builders could build without them. Power, light, air and sparks arrive on four trailers: the support-crew lesson that ends the class where construction-05 began it, deeper.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a torch on a chair (the light tower) and the sound hunt: the generator HUMS, the compressor PSHHH-es, the welder BZZZ-es.

Why this matters

The site has a soundtrack — hum, pshhh, bzzz — and each sound is a machine feeding the others. Children who can hear the support crew can hear how work really works.

What it teaches

Sound-to-machine mapping, power-source thinking (where does site electricity COME FROM?), night-shift wonder (light towers), and the support-first idea, completed.

Words to learn

generatorlight towercompressorwelding truckpowersparkshum

Say this to your child

“"Generator — hummm, the site’s electricity! Light tower — lamps UP, night turns to day! Compressor — pshhh, air for the tools! Welding truck — bzzz, sparks join the steel! None of them build — and none of the builders could build without them. Support first!"”

Step by step

  1. The crew: "generator — HUMMM, it makes the electricity! Light tower — lifts its lamps, night becomes day! Compressor — PSHHH, squeezed air for the tools. Welding truck — BZZZ, joins steel with sparks!"
  2. The sound hunt: make the three sounds — "which machine says each?"
  3. The night question: "how do builders work at night? The light tower — lamps up, site glowing."
  4. The power source: "no plugs on a building site — the GENERATOR makes the electricity. It hums so everything else can work."
  5. The closing idea: "remember the support fleet? This is its heart: before the builders build, someone brings the power. The support crew comes FIRST."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the heading "Construction Vehicles" sits over a generator trailer, a light tower raised, a compressor trailer and a welding truck — the power crew, humming.

Ask your child

"Which machine hums?" (generator) "Which turns night to day?" (light tower) "Which makes sparks?" (the welder) "Who comes first?" (support!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might hum-generate through the house, torch-tower every dark corner, or bzzz-weld toy steel — the soundtrack, running.

Out in the real world

Every site hums, glows, hisses and sparks after dark — drive past one at night and the whole card is audible. Generators also power festivals and film sets.

Try it together

Night Shift: torch light-tower, hum the generator, pshhh the compressor, bzzz-weld the toy frames (spark fingers) — build a block tower BY LAMPLIGHT. The site, powered by its crew.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the power crew." "What does the generator make?" (electricity!) "What did we learn about support?" (it comes first!) — hum, glow, pshhh, bzzz: the class closes on its quietest heroes.

This lesson pairs with the Generator, Light Tower, Compressor & Welding Truck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Transportation & Vehicles (Class 24).
